Raymond III was born around 1140 to Raymond II of Tripoli and Hodierna of Jerusalem. He was the eldest son and heir apparent. His mother was daughter of King Baldwin II of Jerusalem. He grew up in the Crusader state of Tripoli and received training in warfare and diplomacy. His early years were marked by the instability of the region and the frequent clashes between Muslim and Christian forces.

*Reign as Count*
Raymond III succeeded his father as Count of Tripoli in 1152 after Raymond II was assassinated by the Hashashin. He ruled a strategically important coastal county that lay between the Principality of Antioch and the Kingdom of Jerusalem. During his reign he sought to balance alliances with neighboring Christian states and with Muslim powers such as Damascus and Egypt. He participated in the Second Crusade and supported King Louis VII of France during the campaign. Raymond also negotiated treaties with the Ayyubids to secure trade routes. He faced internal challenges from rival nobles and external pressure from the growing power of Saladin. In 1187 he led the Tripoli contingent at the Battle of Hattin where the Crusader army suffered a devastating defeat. Raymond was captured and held prisoner for several years. His captivity weakened his authority and allowed Saladin to take control of many Crusader holdings.

*Death and Legacy*
After his release Raymond III returned to Tripoli but found his county greatly diminished. He died in 1187 shortly after his return possibly from illness or wounds sustained during captivity. His death marked the end of an era for the County of Tripoli which soon fell under Muslim control. Raymond is remembered as a leader who tried to navigate the complex politics of the Crusader states. His efforts to maintain Tripoli independence are noted by historians. His lineage continued through his descendants who held titles in exile. The story of Raymond III illustrates the challenges faced by Crusader nobility in the twelfth century.
